strengths: Simple, elegant, and non-intrusive method: GradPower requires only a single-line elementwise transformation on gradients before passing them to the base optimizer, introducing virtually zero computational overhead (0.4%) and requiring no changes to optimizer states or hyperparameters.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated on both dense (LLaMA from 66M to 2B) and Mixture-of-Experts (Qwen2MoE from 0.5B to 2B) models, across two datasets (C4, OpenWebText) and two common LR schedules (cosine, WSD), as well as zero-shot downstream benchmarks.
Orthogonality and modularity: The paper demonstrates that GradPower can be seamlessly combined with other modern optimization techniques (Muon and Blockwise LR), yielding additive performance gains.

Insightful analysis of noise regimes: The paper uncovers a clear relationship between gradient noise (batch size) and the optimal exponent p—specifically showing why p > 1 is optimal under high noise / standard batch sizes while p < 1 emerges in low-noise regimes. This is supported both empirically and through an illustrative toy case study and convergence proofs for AdagradPower.
weaknesses: Training scale and duration: Experiments are conducted following standard academic compute budgets (up to 2B parameters with Chinchilla token budgets and sequence length 256 on C4). Evaluating whether the observed advantages hold over very long training runs (e.g., trillions of tokens) and sequence lengths typical of frontier models remains to be established.

Theoretical simplifications: The convergence analysis is developed for Adagrad rather than AdamW, which is a common simplification in optimization literature but leaves a gap regarding the interplay between power transformations, exponential moving averages (beta_1, beta_2), and decoupled weight decay.

Comparability of convergence rates in different norms: In Theorem 5.8 (low-noise regime), the convergence rate is established for the \ell_{p+1}^{p+1} norm rather than the \ell_2^2 norm. Claiming a direct 2/(p+1) acceleration over standard Adagrad by comparing with a Jensen-derived bound can be misleading due to dimension-dependent norm equivalences.

Practical rule for setting p at large batch sizes: Figure 6 (right) shows that the optimal p shifts below 1 when batch sizes scale up to 4096 or 8192. Given that industrial pre-training pipelines often employ very large batch sizes, practical heuristics or dynamic schedules for setting p as batch sizes scale would enhance usability.

strengths: Simplicity and practical utility: GradPower requires only a single-line modification to transform the stochastic gradient vector before feeding it to existing optimizers (such as AdamW or Muon), with negligible wall-clock computational overhead (~0.4%).

Thorough empirical evaluation across diverse LLM configurations: The authors evaluate dense models (LLaMA 66M to 2B) and mixture-of-experts models (Qwen2MoE up to 2B), multiple datasets (C4, OpenWebText), and schedules (Cosine, Warmup-Stable-Decay). AdamWPower consistently outperforms tuned AdamW baselines.

Strong hyperparameter transferability: The exponent p = 1.2 tuned on a small 0.2B model transfers robustly across model scales, architectures, and schedules without requiring extensive per-model hyperparameter tuning.
Orthogonality and modularity: The approach is successfully composed with other modern LLM optimization techniques, demonstrating additive improvements when paired with Blockwise LR and Muon.

Insightful connection between gradient noise, batch size, and the power exponent: Both empirical sweeps (across batch sizes in LLMs and CIFAR-10) and an illustrative 1D toy model clearly demonstrate that the optimal p shifts from p > 1 in high-noise regimes to p < 1 in low-noise regimes.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively modest: The coordinate-wise sign-power transformation has appeared in prior optimization literature (notably the Powerball method family), though primarily restricted to SGD/GD on smaller benchmarks with p < 1. The main contribution here is empirical and contextual (adapting to modern adaptive LLM pre-training with p > 1).

Gaps in the theoretical analysis: The convergence analysis is developed for Adagrad rather than AdamW or Muon, and relies on restrictive assumptions (such as R < 1 and Assumption 5.9). Furthermore, Example 5.10 assumes odd integer exponents to satisfy the noise condition, whereas the practical method operates with fractional powers (such as p = 1.2).

Downstream gains are modest: While validation loss consistently improves across pre-training runs, the downstream zero-shot evaluations on common benchmarks (Table 1) show only marginal average improvements (48.26 vs. 47.72) and a slight drop on ARC-Challenge.

Asymmetric learning rate tuning: The peak learning rate was tuned on the AdamW baseline and directly transferred to AdamWPower. Because the nonlinear transformation scales gradient magnitudes entering the moment accumulators, a joint tuning of learning rate for AdamWPower across all settings would provide an even more rigorous comparison.

strengths: Simplicity and ease of adoption: GradPower is conceptually straightforward and requires only a single elementwise gradient transformation before optimizer updates, adding virtually negligible wall-clock overhead (~0.4%).

Extensive empirical evaluation: The authors conduct comprehensive pre-training experiments across diverse settings, including dense LLaMA architectures (66M to 2B) and MoE architectures (Qwen2MoE up to 2B), across two datasets (C4, OpenWebText) and two learning rate schedulers (cosine and WSD).
Consistent scaling improvements: Scaling law curves (Figure 1) demonstrate consistent compute-efficiency advantages over standard AdamW across multiple orders of magnitude of compute.

Orthogonality and transferability: The default exponent p = 1.2 tuned on a small 200M model transfers reliably to larger models and different architectures without retuning. Furthermore, GradPower demonstrates good compatibility when combined with Blockwise LR and Muon.

Insightful analysis of batch size and noise dependence: The observation and toy-model analysis showing that optimal p transitions from p > 1 in high-noise/small-batch regimes to p < 1 in low-noise/large-batch regimes provides useful intuition for practitioner usage.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty relative to prior literature: The elementwise power transformation on gradients is methodologically identical to the Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019; Baiesi, 2019; Zhou et al., 2020). While the paper provides valuable modern scaling experiments and highlights the p > 1 regime for LLMs, the core algorithmic mechanism itself is not new.

Modest downstream task improvements: In Table 1, the downstream zero-shot evaluation on LLaMA (2B) shows only marginal gains over AdamW (48.26% vs. 47.72% average accuracy), with performance slightly dropping on ARC-C (26.28% vs. 26.45%).

Subtleties and limitations in the convergence rate comparison: In Theorem 5.8 (low-noise regime), the convergence bound is stated in terms of min_t E[||\nabla L(\theta_t)||_{p+1}^{p+1}], whereas standard Adagrad bounds min_t E[||\nabla L(\theta_t)||_2^2]. Claiming that AdagradPower is 2/(p+1) times faster is an apples-to-oranges comparison across different L_q norms and exponent scales.

Strong theoretical assumptions: The convergence analysis relies on specialized assumptions (Assumptions 5.6 and 5.9) regarding the alignment of powered stochastic gradients with the true gradient, which are verified only on stylized distributions (e.g., symmetric binary noise with odd integer p). Additionally, the theoretical proofs analyze Adagrad rather than the momentum-based AdamW used in all main experiments.

Interaction with epsilon and gradient magnitude: Because typical LLM gradients are small (|g| << 1), applying |g|^p with p = 1.2 significantly dampens raw gradient scales. In adaptive optimizers, this strongly changes the relative dominance of the numerical stability parameter epsilon in the denominator. The paper would benefit from a more explicit ablation disentangling the power transformation from an effective epsilon / learning rate rescaling.
